title: Classroom Chairs, Coercion, and the Right to Concentrate
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Kirschner responds to Neil Selwyn's critique of the modern classroom chair as a tool of 'coercive design'. He grants that chairs are not neutral and that furniture companies overclaim, but argues that Selwyn treats shaping pupil behaviour as inherently suspect when some constraint is a precondition for teaching. His central move is to separate bad coercion (humiliation, restraint, hostile rooms) from legitimate structure: routines, seating plans and adult authority that protect attention. He ties this to the progressive assumption that pupil choice is inherently liberating, countering that novices are poor judges of what helps them learn and that permissive classrooms hurt quieter, anxious and less knowledgeable pupils most. The piece reads as a classroom-order and school-culture argument rather than a pedagogy or ed-tech one, and closes by saying furniture should be judged by whether it helps teachers teach and pupils learn.
points: Kirschner agrees that classroom objects embody assumptions and that commercial learning-space claims deserve scepticism, since a chair is not a pedagogy.
He distinguishes harmful coercion from the legitimate structure of routines, norms, seating plans and adult authority that make concentration possible.
Pupil preference is not the same as what is good for learning, so novices cannot be left to steer their own conditions.
Permissive classrooms distribute costs unequally, favouring confident or knowledgeable pupils while the quiet, anxious or special-needs pupil loses out.
The right test for furniture and room design is whether it helps pupils attend and helps teachers teach, not whether it maximises choice.
quotes: A chair may support certain classroom routines, but it isn’t a pedagogy. It can’t replace curriculum, instruction, explanation, practice, feedback, or classroom management.
But in schooling, not all constraint is bad. In fact, some constraint is necessary. A classroom isn’t simply a space for individual expression.
They may know what they prefer or what feels comfortable, enjoyable, or immediately rewarding. But preference isn’t the same as what’s good for learning.
A room full of mobile chairs doesn’t produce collaboration. A stool that lets pupils swivel doesn’t produce attention. A “learning zone” doesn’t produce learning.
These conditions don’t emerge automatically from freedom. They require routines, norms, seating plans, and adult authority.

A teacher who insists on order isn’t necessarily being authoritarian. They may be protecting the learning rights of the whole class. The freedom of one child to interrupt can become a coercive force imposed on everyone else.

But classrooms are places for learning, and learning often requires structure. Furniture should be judged not by whether it maximises pupil choice or avoids all constraint, but by whether it helps teachers teach and pupils learn.
